title: How do you film a product demo so it looks real?
description: How to film a UGC product demo that looks real: one continuous take for the key moment, your hands in frame, everyday settings and results shown at real speed.
short_answer: A product demo looks real when the key moment happens in one continuous take, in your own hands, in the place you would really use the product. Keep the camera rolling from before the product touches anything until after the result, leave the speed alone, and let small imperfections stay in the shot.

sections.heading: What makes a product demo look staged instead of real?

blocks.text: A demo looks staged when the viewer cannot see cause and effect in one unbroken shot, so they have to trust a cut instead of their eyes.

Picture a stain remover demo where the stained shirt is shown, then there is a cut, then a clean shirt appears. Nothing on screen proves the second shirt is the first one. Other signs a viewer reads as staged are a spotless set nobody lives in, hands that never touch the product, and lighting that changes between the before and after. The fix for each is the same idea: film the moment the way you would show a friend, without stopping.

Plan the demo before you press record. Writing what you say and what the camera sees side by side, as in [the two-column script](/blog/two-column-script/), shows you which line has to land inside the unbroken take and which lines can be filmed separately.

sections.heading: Which part of the demo needs one continuous take?

blocks.text: The moment the product does its job needs one continuous take, from a second before it starts to a second after the result is visible.

Everything around that moment can be cut freely: the [hook](/glossary/#hook), the setup, the close and any [B-roll](/blog/ugc-b-roll/). Only the proof has to be unbroken. Mark it in your [shot list](/glossary/#shot-list) as the one shot you cannot fake, and film it several times so you have a clean take to choose from.

table_head: Where the take starts and ends
table_rows: Opening it and setting a phone on it
Stand closed in your hand, ends with the phone resting at eye level
One pass over a jumper covered in pet hair
Hair visible on the fabric, ends with the roller held up to the lens
Kettle lifted from the hob, ends with the stream stopping cleanly
Clothes in a heap, ends with the zip pulled shut

sections.heading: Why should your hands be in the frame?

blocks.text: Hands in the frame prove a person is using the product right now, which is the whole point of a demo filmed by a creator rather than a studio.

items: Film over your shoulder or from your chest so the viewer sees what you see, because that angle feels like their own hands.
Keep your hands slightly slower than normal, since quick movements blur on a phone and hide the detail you want seen.
Leave your hands as they are on a normal day, but wash them and clear anything distracting like a plaster or a bright ring.
Show one small fumble if it happens, such as a lid that sticks, because a real hand meeting a real object is what the viewer believes.

blocks.text: If you are filming alone, a phone clamped above the counter frees both hands. [How to film UGC on a phone so it looks good](/blog/film-ugc-on-a-phone/) covers framing and focus in more detail.

sections.heading: Where should you film a product demo?

blocks.text: Film it where you would really use the product, in the light that place really has, because a believable setting does half the work of a demo.

A kettle belongs on your hob with yesterday's mug beside it, and a backpack belongs by your front door. Tidy enough that the product is the clearest thing in the shot, but do not clear the room into a showroom. If the real place is dark, add light instead of moving somewhere prettier: [how to light a UGC video at home](/blog/light-ugc-at-home/) shows how to do that with a window and a lamp. Keep the lighting the same through the before and after, because a change in light between them looks like an edit even when it is not one.

sections.heading: How do you show results without speeding them up?

blocks.text: Show the result at real speed and choose a demo that fits the time you have, rather than speeding up footage or cutting the slow part out of the proof.

items: Pick the fastest true result the product has, such as the first pass of the roller, instead of the full job.
If the result takes longer, film the start and the end in the same frame with a visible clock or a changed window light, and say plainly how long it was.
Keep any speed-up for the setup or the B-roll, and leave the proof shot untouched.
Never swap in a second product, a cleaner surface or a result you did not film, and ask the brand in writing how it wants any time gap shown.

blocks.text: Your words matter as much as the footage. Say what you noticed, in the order you noticed it, and let the [payoff](/glossary/#payoff) be the thing the viewer has just watched happen. If the hook promised more than the demo shows, rewrite the hook, as [hook and payoff](/blog/hook-payoff/) explains.

sections.heading: What should you check before you send the demo to the brand?

blocks.text: Watch it once with the sound off and ask whether the product's job is clear from the picture alone, because that is the test a real demo passes.

items: The proof shot runs without a cut from before to after.
Your hands appear in that shot, and the product's label or shape is readable at least once.
The light and setting match across the before and after.
Your spoken lines describe what you saw, not what the product does for everyone.
Your sound is clear enough to follow, which [how to get clear audio in a UGC video](/blog/ugc-audio/) helps with.
